judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are Indicators (same grain) under the same Content Standard B4.3.3.2 'Demonstrate an understanding of area of regular and irregular 2-D shapes' in Sub-Strand 'Measurement- (Perimeter and Area)', and both carry the resolved Grade coordinate BASIC 4 (rank 0). B4.3.3.2.2 (second) covers selecting and justifying referents for the square units cm² and m² (LCs: 'Select referents for the units cm² or m²', 'Justify referents for the units cm² or m²'); B4.3.3.2.4 (first) covers developing and applying a formula for the area of a rectangle and square (LCs: 'Develop a formula...', 'Apply a formula...'). These are substantively coherent, complementary components of measuring area in square units — unit referents give meaning to the cm²/m² in which formula-derived areas are expressed — which is more than generic repetition or reusable LC overlap. However, the evidence does not support a developmental dependency at equal rank: referent selection/justification is a benchmark-and-estimation skill whose visible in-standard target is the sibling indicator B4.3.3.2.3 ('Estimate area by using referents for cm2 or m2', seen in the retained source_context_labels), while formula development rests on unit-square/array reasoning (B4.3.3.2.1 'Recognise that area is measured in square units'). The remaining nomination signals (shared ancestors, shared tag 'area', stop-word token/trigram overlap, weak code prefix, weak page proximity) are explicitly weak or generic and cannot by themselves license buildsTowards in either direction. Canonical symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the supported judgment; endpoint order is technical only. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and all endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, which is retained and did not alter this judgment.

B4.2.2.2.1 is concrete solving of a given one-step equation with manipulatives (LC tags: equation, manipulatives, one-step, solve). B4.2.2.2.6 requires both representing and solving an addition/subtraction word problem in a part-part-whole or comparison context using a symbol for the unknown (LCs split represent/solve; tags include symbol, unknown, addition, subtraction). This is a substantive extension: from solving an already-given equation with concrete materials to modelling a contextual problem symbolically and then solving it, so proficiency with the manipulative-based one-step solving supports success on the applied symbolic representation task. Same-rank direction rests on this content shift, not on the .1/.6 code order or shared parent alone; the modest evidence base (shared tokens 'solve','given','using' are generic) keeps confidence moderate.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Content Standards (same statement-type grain, rank 0, canonical value 'BASIC 4') under Sub-Strand 1 'Counting, Representation & Cardinality' in Strand 1 NUMBER. B4.1.1.1 covers quantities and place value for multi-digit whole numerals up to 100,000; B4.1.1.2 covers the Roman numeral system up to XXX (30), whose bounded source context includes counting and converting Hindu-Arabic numerals to Roman numerals and vice versa. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators in Strand 2 Algebra, Sub-strand 'Unknowns, Expressions and Equations' (same statement-type grain, same coordinate rank 0). B4.2.2.1.2 asks learners to translate a pictorial or concrete representation into a symbolic equation, establishing the meaning of the symbolic form and of the symbol standing for an unknown (parent Content Standard B4.2.2.1: express a given problem as an equation with a symbol for an unknown). B4.2.2.2.7 reverses and extends that translation: learners must read a given equation with one unknown and generate a matching problem situation (parent Content Standard B4.2.2.2: solve one-step equations involving a symbol for an unknown). Facility in mapping concrete/pictorial situations onto symbolic equations substantively supports the more demanding inverse task of inventing a valid contextual problem for a given symbolic equation, so a same-rank forward direction from the representation-to-symbol skill to the equation-to-problem skill is supported by the statement text and LC tags ('equation', 'representation', 'symbolic form' vs 'equation', 'unknown', 'problem'). Confidence is moderated because both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and their source evidence excerpts are truncated (24 omitted evidence items each), and the shared lexical/code-prefix signals alone would not establish direction.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (same grain, rank 1) under Content Standard B5.1.1.1 'Demonstrate an understanding of quantities and place value for multi-digit numerals up to 1000,000' in Strand 1-Number, Sub-strand Counting, Representation & Cardinality. The second SFI (B5.1.1.1.1) has learners model number quantities up to 1,000,000 with graph sheets and multi-base blocks, building concrete place-value structure (LC tags 'place value', 'modelling', 'multi-base block'). The first SFI (B5.1.1.1.5) requires rounding off/up/down whole numbers up to 100,000 to the nearest ten thousands, thousands, hundreds and tens, which presupposes fluency in identifying and comparing place-value positions; its LCs are also tagged 'place value'. Proficiency in representing/modelling multi-digit quantities therefore supports success in place-value-dependent rounding, a substantive same-rank developmental direction rather than mere shared parent or code-prefix overlap. Direction asserted at same rank on this conceptual dependency, not on source code order; evidence for both endpoints is bounded by truncated source excerpts and upstream merge context on the shared Content Standard and Grade organizers, which tempers confidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 (rank 1) Indicators under the same Algebra / Patterns and Relationships Content Standard B5.2.1.1 ('Determine the pattern rule to make predictions about subsequent elements'), so direction rests on substantive content, not code order or shared parentage. B5.2.1.1.6 asks learners to determine and explain why a given number is or is not the next element in a pattern (LCs: determine next element; explain/reasoning), which requires identifying and justifying the pattern's rule in an informal, case-based way. B5.2.1.1.7 requires expressing that rule generally, first in words and then symbolically in algebra (LCs: write a rule in words; write a rule in algebra), an increase in abstraction and generalization. Proficiency in recognising and justifying the governing rule for particular elements plausibly supports success in formally stating that rule verbally and algebraically, supporting a same-rank first_to_second developmental direction. Evidence limitation: both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each), so the judgment rests on the bounded statement text and LCs.

judgment.rationale: Both are Content Standards at the same grain, same canonical coordinate BASIC 4 (rank 0), under Sub-Strand 3: Fractions in Strand 1: NUMBER, so direction rests on statement content rather than rank. B4.1.3.1 establishes understanding of equivalent (and improper) fractions; B4.1.3.2 requires strategies for comparing, adding and subtracting fractions where 'one [denominator] being a multiple of the others', which operationally depends on generating and recognising equivalent fractions to rename terms before comparison or addition. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, same Grade coordinate) under Strand 3 Geometry and Measurement, but in different Sub-Strands: B5.3.1.1.2 (Lines and Shapes) uses paper folding on cut-out squares and rectangles to investigate side, angle and diagonal properties, while B5.3.3.3.1 (Measurement - Angles) identifies environmental angles equal to, less than, or greater than a right angle. Their LCs share genuine conceptual coherence around angle properties: investigating the angles of squares/rectangles (right angles) reinforces and is reinforced by recognising right, acute and obtuse angles in real contexts. However, neither statement's evidence shows one as a substantive extension or dependency of the other (shape-attribute investigation vs. angle comparison/classification), and the same-rank placement provides no developmental direction, so symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than buildsTowards. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), limiting confirmation of exemplar-level overlap.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 6 Indicators (same grain, same rank 2) under Strand 1: Number / Sub-Strand 2: Number Operations. The first (B6.1.2.1.1) develops mental-mathematics strategies and number properties to determine basic multiplication facts to 81 and the related division facts, with LCs on skip counting, doubling/halving, repeated doubling/halving and 9s/11s patterns. The second (B6.1.2.4.1, under Content Standard B6.1.2.4 on division of 2- or 3-digit numbers by 1- or 2-digit numbers) requires dividing 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number 'efficiently'. Recall and flexible use of basic division facts is the substantive underpinning of efficient multi-digit division procedures, so proficiency in the first supports success in the second; the change is from single-fact recall/mental strategy to applying it within multi-digit division. Same-rank direction rests on this pair-specific content dependency, not on code prefix or shared ancestors alone (the nomination's lexical overlap evidence is weak: shared tokens 'division'/'number' only). Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, limiting exemplar detail.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (rank 0) under the same Content Standard B4.1.3.1 'Develop an understanding of equivalent and improper fractions' in Sub-strand 3: Fractions. B4.1.3.1.4 extends this same unit-fraction/whole structure past one whole: recognising, drawing and labelling fractions greater than one (improper fractions) with their symbols (LCs: 'Recognise ... improper fractions', 'Draw improper fractions', 'Label improper fractions with their symbols'). judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis) under the same Content Standard B4.4.1.1 on many-to-one correspondence in displaying and interpreting graphs, so the grain matches. Beyond shared placement, the statement texts show a pair-specific developmental step: the first (B4.4.1.1.2, LC 'use an understanding of many-to-one correspondence to display or construct graphs') develops the productive skill of constructing/displaying graphs with a many-to-one scale, while the second (B4.4.1.1.3, LCs 'compare graphs in which the same data has been displayed' and 'explain how graphs displaying the same data are the same and different') requires analysing and justifying differences among multiple completed displays of the same data set. Fluency in constructing such graphs and understanding their scale conventions plausibly supports success in comparing and explaining alternative displays, so the forward direction is first_to_second; the reverse is not supported since comparison presupposes familiarity with how the displays are built. Evidence is limited to bounded excerpts with per-SFI source-evidence truncation (24 omitted items each), but the retained statement text and Learning Components are sufficient and non-contradictory.

judgment.rationale: B5.1.1.1 addresses quantities and place value for multi-digit Hindu-Arabic numerals (up to 100,000/1,000,000), while B5.1.1.2 addresses understanding Roman Numerals up to C (100). Both sit at the same BASIC 5 coordinate (rank 1) under Strand 1 - Number, Sub-strand 1: Counting, Representation & Cardinality, and are the same statement grain (Content Standard). They are coherent complementary numeration/representation topics — reading and interpreting numeral systems — but the Roman-numeral standard is a distinct, non-positional system limited to 100 and is not a substantive extension or deepening of multi-digit place value; no evidence supports one being required for or developmentally supporting success in the other within the same grade. The shared token/trigram overlap is largely generic stem wording ('demonstrate an understanding of ... numerals up to'), and the code-prefix/page-proximity signals are weak sequencing artefacts rather than developmental evidence, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment. Note the first endpoint carries a merge decision resolving a stale 'CONT'D' duplicate of B5.1.1.1, and both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (43 and 24 omitted items), which bounds but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 (rank 1) Indicators in the Number strand: B5.1.4.1.5 asks learners to use models to explain multiplying a decimal (to thousandths) by a whole number, while B5.1.5.1.1 asks them to determine the percentage of a given quantity (2-digit whole number) and vice versa. There is genuine conceptual coherence — percentages are a decimal/part-of-a-whole representation and finding a percentage of a quantity is commonly carried out as a decimal-by-whole-number multiplication — so the two reinforce each other meaningfully. However, they sit under different Content Standards (B5.1.4.1 decimal fractions vs B5.1.5.1 percentage), share the same grade rank, and the nomination evidence is only weak local-rank/code-prefix/page proximity plus generic token overlap ('a', 'number', 'of', 'the', 'to', 'whole'), which is insufficient to assert a same-rank developmental direction in either orientation. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment; note that both endpoints carry unresolved ancestry and truncated source evidence, so hierarchy was not used as positive placement evidence.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, identical coordinate) under the same Content Standard B5.1.1.3 on factors, multiples, composite, even, odd and prime numbers 1-100, in the Number strand / Counting, Representation & Cardinality sub-strand. B5.1.1.3.3 classifies numbers 1-100 as even or odd via whether they can be arrayed in twos; B5.1.1.3.2 generates and identifies prime and composite numbers 1-100. These are complementary classification schemes for the same number range, mutually reinforcing divisibility/array reasoning, but the bounded evidence gives no substantive same-rank developmental dependency: neither statement's exemplification requires the other, and the source code ordering (3.2 before 3.3) runs opposite to any even/odd-to-prime/composite inference, so a directional buildsTowards is not warranted. Endpoint source evidence is truncated and both endpoints and ancestors carry upstream audit/merge context, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are same-grain Content Standards on basic division facts. The second (B5.1.2.3, BASIC 5, rank 1) requires recall of basic division facts up to 100; the first (B6.1.2.3, BASIC 6, rank 2) requires manipulating numbers using basic division facts up to 144, extending both the fact range and the cognitive demand from recall to manipulation/application. Lower-to-higher configured BASIC 5 to BASIC 6 direction supports second_to_first: fluency in recalling division facts to 100 supports success in manipulating numbers with facts to 144. The BASIC 6 item sits under Strand 1: Number / Sub-Strand 2: Number Operations; the BASIC 5 item has unresolved ancestry, so its framework-root fallback was not used as placement evidence — the judgment rests on its own statement text, code, and resolved BASIC 5 grade coordinate. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated, which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (rank 2) under the same Content Standard B6.1.1.2 'Demonstrate understanding of Roman Numerals up to C (i.e. 100)', so shared hierarchy alone is not decisive; the substantive same-rank evidence is in the statement text. B6.1.1.2.1 asks learners to recognise the Roman numeral system up to C, while B6.1.1.2.2 requires counting and converting Hindu Arabic numbers to Roman numerals up to 100 (C) 'and vice versa', with Learning Components covering bidirectional conversion. Recognising the symbols and structure of the Roman numeral system is the enabling proficiency for accurately converting in both directions, so the first supports likely success in the second within the same grade band. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, same Grade coordinate) under the same Content Standard B5.2.3.1 'Solve problems involving single-variable, one-step equations with whole number coefficients' in Strand 2 Algebra / Sub-Strand 3 Variables and Equations, so the grain and topic match. B5.2.3.1.2 requires identifying the unknown, representing a problem with an equation, and solving it concretely, pictorially or symbolically (LCs: identify the unknown; represent the problem with an equation; solve concretely/pictorially/symbolically). B5.2.3.1.3 requires creating a problem for a given equation (LC: create a problem for a given equation). This is the inverse, problem-posing task: fluency in translating a situation into an equation and solving it substantively supports success in generating a contextual problem that matches a given equation, giving same-rank developmental direction from the modelling/solving indicator to the problem-creation indicator rather than mere shared parentage, code prefix, or page proximity.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Content Standards (same statement-type grain, identical rank 0) under Strand 1: NUMBER, but in different sub-strands: B4.1.3.1 'Develop an understanding of equivalent and improper fractions' (Sub-strand 3: Fractions) and B4.1.1.3 'Demonstrate an understanding of factors, multiples and squared numbers' (Sub-strand 1: Counting, Representation & Cardinality). There is genuine conceptual coherence — multiplicative reasoning with factors and multiples underlies generating and recognising equivalent fractions and converting improper fractions — so this is more than shared-parent or token overlap (the nominated overlap was only generic words such as 'an', 'and', 'of', 'understanding' and the weak shared 'b4.1' code prefix). However, the bounded evidence contains no learning components and only truncated source evidence (the visible B4.1.3.1 indicator concerns unit fractions on a number line), so it does not substantiate a same-rank developmental dependency in either direction; symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment.

The pair-specific evidence supports it: B6.1.3.1.1 requires comparing and ordering a mixture of common, percent and decimal fractions (LCs 'Compare a mixture of fractions...' and 'Order a mixture of fractions...'), which depends on recognising equivalence and rewriting fractions to a common form; B6.1.3.1.2 extends that same equivalence work into operations on unlike and mixed fractions (LCs 'Add unlike and mixed fractions', 'Subtract unlike and mixed fractions'). judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (rank 2) under Strand 1: Number / Sub-Strand 2: Number Operations, so direction rests on statement content, not rank. The second SFI (B6.1.2.1.2) asks learners to apply mental mathematics strategies for multiplication — annexing then adding zero, halving and doubling, and the distributive property — under a Content Standard about basic multiplication facts to 144 and related division facts; its Learning Components isolate each of these strategies. The first SFI (B6.1.2.2.1) requires multiplying multi-digit numbers by 2 or 3-digit numbers 'efficiently', under a Content Standard on multiplication of 2/3-digit by 2/3-digit numbers. Fluency with the distributive property, annexing zeros, and doubling/halving is exactly what supports efficient multi-digit multiplication of larger factors, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first; the change is from strategy/fact-level mental methods to their application on larger multi-digit computations. Same-grade, same-sub-strand placement and shared 'multiplication' LC tagging corroborate substantive coherence rather than mere wording overlap.

The second SFI (B4.1.1.3.1) asks learners to determine the set of factors of a given number up to 50; the first (B4.1.1.3.2) asks learners to determine the highest common factor of any two whole numbers between 1 and 50. Generating a complete factor set for a single number is the enabling skill that is then extended to two numbers and to comparing/selecting the greatest shared factor, a substantive increase in complexity within the same 1-50 number range (LC tags 'factors'/'numbers' vs 'factors'/'hcf'). Proficiency with factor sets therefore supports success with HCF, giving buildsTowards from the second endpoint to the first.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 5 Indicators (same grain, same rank 1) under Strand 1 Number / Sub-strand 1 Counting, Representation & Cardinality, but sit under different Content Standards: B5.1.1.1 (place value and quantities to 1,000,000) yields 'Read and write numbers in figures and in words up to 1000,000' (LCs: read/write numbers in figures and words), while B5.1.1.2 (Roman Numerals to C) yields 'Count and convert Hindu Arabic numbers to Roman numerals up to 100 (C) and vice versa' (LCs: count Hindu Arabic numbers to 100, convert both directions). They cohere substantively as complementary ways of representing and naming whole numbers (figures/words vs. Roman symbols), and the Hindu-Arabic counting/notation work reinforces the conversion task. However, the Roman numeral indicator operates only up to 100 and depends on far simpler numeral knowledge than reading/writing to 1,000,000, so the shared-rank evidence does not substantiate a directional developmental dependency in either direction; token/code-prefix overlap ('numbers', 'up to', B5.1.1) is weak and non-semantic. Symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 (Solve one-step equations involving a symbol for an unknown) in Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations, at the same BASIC 4 coordinate (rank 0), so direction rests on statement content, not rank. B4.2.2.2.3 (first) asks learners to solve an already-given equation with the unknown on either side — a bounded procedural skill (LC: 'Solve a given equation when the unknown is on the left or right side of the equation'). B4.2.2.2.5 (second) requires the added modelling steps of identifying the unknown in a problem, representing that problem with an equation, and then solving it concretely, pictorially or symbolically (LCs: 'Identify the unknown in a problem', 'Represent the problem with an equation', 'Solve the problem concretely, pictorially or symbolically'). The second combines and extends the first: fluency in solving a supplied equation with the unknown in either position supports success when learners must first construct the equation from a problem and then solve it across representations. This is a same-grade substantive extension rather than mere repetition, so buildsTowards first_to_second is supported; endpoint source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), which tempers confidence slightly.

B6.4.1.2.1 requires choosing and justifying a data-collection method to answer a given question (LCs: 'Select a method for collecting data to answer a given question'; 'Justify the choice of data collection method'), while B6.4.1.1.3 requires drawing a line graph from a given table of values and answering questions to interpret and draw conclusions (LCs: 'Draw a line graph for a given table of values'; 'Answer questions based on a line graph to interpret it and draw conclusions'). judgment.rationale: Same-grain Content Standard pair, both resolved to Grade coordinate BASIC 5 (rank 1) under Strand 2 ALGEBRA but in distinct sub-strands (Patterns and Relationships vs Algebraic Expressions). Canonical symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the complete judgment. Confidence is tempered by truncated source evidence at both endpoints (34 and 24 omitted items), absent Learning Components, and the retained upstream audit/merge/code warnings on both endpoints and their Strand, Sub-Strand, and Grade ancestors (the Grade organizer BASIC 5 is a merged node).

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 (rank 1) Indicators under the same Content Standard B5.2.1.1 'Determine the pattern rule to make predictions about subsequent elements' (Algebra / Patterns and Relationships), so the grain and topic match. Same-rank direction is justified by substantive pair-specific content: B5.2.1.1.1 (second) has learners extend a given pattern with and without concrete materials and explain how each element differs from the preceding one — generating the next element and articulating the element-to-element change. B5.2.1.1.6 (first) requires the more demanding evaluative move of judging and justifying why a proposed number is or is not the next element, i.e. testing a candidate against the pattern rule. Proficiency in extending and describing successive differences directly supports the ability to verify and explain acceptance/rejection of a proposed next element, so the second builds towards the first. Shared LC tokens ('pattern', 'explain', 'element') reflect this genuine conceptual continuity rather than generic wording alone; source-code prefix and rank proximity were treated only as nomination signals. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), but the supplied statement texts and Learning Components are sufficient and non-conflicting.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, same coordinate) under the same Content Standard B5.1.1.1 (quantities and place value for multi-digit numerals) in Strand 1-Number, Sub-strand 1 Counting, Representation & Cardinality. First: skip counting forwards/backwards in 500s, 1000s up to and from 100,000; second: rounding (off/up/down) whole numbers up to 100,000 to nearest ten thousands, thousands, hundreds and tens. Their LCs share the 'place value' tag and the same 100,000 number range, so they are coherent, mutually reinforcing place-value skills within the same number range (locating and naming multiples vs. approximating to nearest place). Evidence shows no substantive same-rank developmental dependency: rounding does not require skip counting proficiency and vice versa, and shared code prefix, page proximity, and token overlap ('100', '000', 'up', 'to') are weak nomination signals only. Therefore symmetric relatesTo rather than buildsTowards. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each) and ancestors carry merge/audit context (including a stale B5.1.1.1 continuation merge), which limits but does not contradict this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 2 Algebra, Sub-strand 1 Patterns and Relationships, so same-grain comparison applies. B4.2.1.1.3 ('Identify the error(s) in a given table or chart') sits under the Content Standard for identifying and describing patterns found in tables and charts: detecting an error requires reading the table/chart and recognising the governing pattern. B4.2.1.3.2 ('Identify and extend the patterns in a table or chart to solve a given problem') sits under the Content Standard for representing, describing and extending patterns using charts and tables to solve problems, and its Learning Components separate 'identify the patterns...' from 'extend the patterns... to solve a given problem'. The second thus retains the same identification-in-a-table/chart skill and adds extension plus application to a problem, a substantive increase in complexity, so proficiency in the error-detection indicator supports success in the extension/problem-solving indicator. Shared LC tokens (chart, table, patterns) and the common code prefix alone were not treated as sufficient; the pair-specific skill overlap and added extension/application step carry the judgment. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so this direction rests on the bounded statement, LC, and hierarchy text supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (same grade rank 2) within Strand 1: Number, Sub-Strand 4: Ratios and Proportion, so the pair is judged at the same statement-type grain. The second SFI (B6.1.4.1.2, LCs: express ratios in equivalent forms, compare ratios, order ratios) sits under Content Standard B6.1.4.1 'Demonstrate understanding of the concept of ratios...'. The first SFI (B6.1.4.2.3, LCs: use various strategies to solve proportional reasoning problems involving rates / involving scales) sits under B6.1.4.2, whose text explicitly frames proportion 'and its relationship to ratios and rates' and applies proportional reasoning to real-world problems. Fluency with equivalent, comparable and ordered ratios substantively supports success in multi-strategy proportional reasoning with rates and scales, giving a same-rank developmental direction from the second to the first rather than mere shared-parent or code-prefix proximity (token/trigram overlap is negligible and was not relied on). Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so this rests on the supplied statements, ancestors and LCs only.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (rank 0, same canonical coordinate) sharing the parent Content Standard B4.3.3.2 'Demonstrate an understanding of area of regular and irregular 2-D shapes' under Sub-strand 3 Measurement (Perimeter and Area). B4.3.3.2.5 asks pupils to construct different rectangles for a given area (cm2 or m2) to show many rectangles share an area; B4.3.3.2.3 asks pupils to estimate area using referents for cm2 or m2. Their LCs confirm substantive shared content: square-unit measures (cm2/m2) applied to area. These are complementary approaches to quantifying area (estimating with unit referents vs. constructing shapes to a target area) rather than a demonstrated dependency; same-rank placement offers no directional evidence, and shared row/page/code prefix alone is not semantic. Symmetric relatesTo is therefore the supported judgment. Both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each), limiting exemplar-level detail.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 4 Indicators (resolved coordinate, rank 0) whose single direct parent is the perimeter Content Standard B4.3.3.1 'Demonstrate understanding of perimeter of regular and irregular shapes' within Sub-Strand 'Measurement- (Perimeter and Area)'. B4.3.3.1.1 estimates perimeter using referents for centimetre or metre; B4.3.3.1.4 constructs different rectangles for a given perimeter (cm, m) to show many shapes share one perimeter. These are substantively coherent, mutually reinforcing facets of perimeter work in the same units and the same instructional standard: estimation builds magnitude sense for boundary length, while construction explores the inverse, non-unique relationship between perimeter and shape. That coherence is pair-specific and useful instructionally, so canonical symmetric relatesTo applies. Developmental dependency is not supported: the two indicators are at the same BASIC 4 rank, and estimation with length referents is not a skill whose proficiency materially supports success at the additive/spatial reasoning of generating several rectangles with a fixed perimeter; the remaining nomination signals (shared parent/ancestors, B4.3.3.1 code prefix, 'perimeter' LC tag and token/trigram overlap, weak rank_gap-0 proximity) cannot by themselves license buildsTowards in either direction. Material limitations retained: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted evidence items each) and both, plus all four ancestors, carry upstream audit/merge/code context arising from the known Basic 4 B4.3.3.1 same-code/different-content collision boundary; this context is audit information only and is not treated as positive placement evidence.

There is genuine pair-specific coherence: graphs located in newspapers, magazines and the internet are precisely the media-sourced (second-hand) data the other indicator asks pupils to characterise, so the two reinforce each other about data sources and their published representations. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1, gap 0), so no rank-based direction is available. B5.2.1.1.5 (Algebra / Patterns and Relationships) asks learners to solve a problem by using a pattern rule to determine subsequent elements; B5.1.1.1.6 (Number / Counting, Representation & Cardinality) asks learners to skip count forwards and backwards in 500s, 1000s up to and from 100,000, with LCs 'skip count forwards...' and 'skip count backwards...'. Skip counting is a concrete constant-difference numeric sequence, so the two statements share genuine conceptual coherence about generating and continuing rule-governed sequences and mutually reinforce sequence reasoning. However, the skip-counting Indicator states a fixed counting routine within place-value understanding rather than deriving or applying a pattern rule to novel problems, and the shared-token evidence is negligible (only 'to'); the evidence does not substantiate a same-rank developmental dependency in either direction, so the symmetric relation is the supported judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same grade rank 0) under Strand 1 NUMBER / Sub-strand 2 Number Operations, so direction rests on substantive content rather than coordinate gap. The second SFI (B4.1.2.1.1) asks learners to determine basic multiplication facts up to 12 × 12 under the Content Standard 'Recall basic multiplication fact up to 12 × 12'; the first SFI (B4.1.2.2.2) asks learners to apply mental mathematics strategies for multiplication — annexing then adding zero, halving and doubling, and the distributive property — under the Content Standard about using mental strategies and number properties to determine answers for basic multiplication facts and related division facts. Its Learning Components (halving/doubling, distributive property, annexing zero for mental multiplication) presuppose command of the underlying fact set that the second SFI establishes, and extend it to strategic derivation of larger or unknown products. Fact fluency therefore supports success with the strategy-based indicator, giving a same-grade developmental direction from the second to the first, not mere shared 'multiplication' wording or code-prefix proximity. Evidence limits: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted source-evidence items each) and both carry upstream audit/merge context, so the judgment rests on the bounded statement text, hierarchy, and LCs supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both are Basic 4 Indicators (rank 0, same canonical coordinate) under the same Sub-Strand 'Measurement- (Perimeter and Area)' in Strand 3, but under different Content Standards: B4.3.3.1.3 develops and applies a perimeter formula for squares and rectangles, while B4.3.3.2.5 constructs different rectangles with a given area to show area is not determined by shape dimensions alone. The LCs ('develop/apply a formula for determining the perimeter of a square and rectangle' vs 'construct different rectangles for a given area') show substantive coherence in reasoning about rectangle side lengths and measurement attributes, and the two attributes are commonly contrasted instructionally. However, the perimeter formula work is not evidenced as supporting success on the area-construction task (and vice versa), and both sit at the same grade rank with no substantive evidence of developmental ordering, so a symmetric relatesTo rather than buildsTowards is warranted. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), limiting deeper exemplar-level evidence.

The second endpoint (B4.1.1.3.1, LC 'Determine the set of factors of a given number up to 50', tags factors/numbers/sets) is a concrete generative skill: producing complete factor sets for bounded numbers. The first endpoint (B4.1.1.3.4, LC 'Recognise the relationship between factors and multiples', tags factors/multiples/relationship) is a more integrative conceptual step that reasons about how the factor relation inverts into the multiple relation, which presupposes being able to identify factors of a number. The first asks learners to tell position and motion of objects in space using north/south/east/west; the second asks them to identify images of a reflection of a 2D shape in a plane. Their LCs share spatial-orientation content (position/motion in space vs. image location after reflection), giving genuine conceptual coherence in describing where objects sit and move in a plane, but neither statement's proficiency is evidenced as supporting success in the other: cardinal-direction naming is not a stated component of identifying reflection images, and the shared-rank placement provides no substantive developmental ordering. Token/trigram, code-prefix and page-proximity signals are weak ('in', 'of') and carry no semantic weight on their own, so symmetric relatesTo rather than buildsTowards is the supported judgment.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (rank 1) under the same Content Standard B5.1.3.1 (comparing, adding, subtracting, multiplying fractions) in Sub-Strand Number: Fractions, so the grain and topic match. Same-rank direction is supported by substantive content difference rather than code order alone: B5.1.3.1.3 establishes using equivalent fractions to change fractions to a common denominator for addition and subtraction of like fractions where one denominator is a multiple of the other (LCs on addition and subtraction with denominator conversion), while B5.1.3.1.4 applies the same equivalent-fraction machinery to the more complex case of fractions greater than one, i.e. improper and mixed fractions (LCs on adding and subtracting improper/mixed fractions). Proficiency in renaming to a common denominator for proper like fractions supports success in adding/subtracting improper and mixed fractions, which additionally requires handling whole-number parts. Audit context confirms the two are distinct curriculum items, not a merge artefact; both endpoints' source evidence is truncated, but the full statement texts and LCs supplied are sufficient for this judgment.

B4.2.1.1.2 ('Determine the missing element(s) in a given table or chart', under Content Standard B4.2.1.1 on identifying and describing patterns found in tables and charts) requires reading the pattern structure encoded in an existing table/chart. B4.2.1.2.2 ('Create a table or chart from a given concrete representation of a pattern', under Content Standard B4.2.1.2 on translating among representations) requires the learner to generate that tabular structure from concrete material, which is a productive extension of first being able to read and complete pattern entries in a table or chart. Proficiency in interpreting and completing given tables/charts therefore supports success in constructing them, so the developmental direction runs second_to_first; the shared table/chart wording alone was not treated as sufficient, and the code-prefix, page-proximity and rank-proximity signals were treated as weak nomination signals only. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 (rank 1) Indicators of the same grain sharing Content Standard B5.1.4.1 ('Demonstrate understanding of decimals fractions and strategies for comparing, adding and subtracting decimal fraction'). B5.1.4.1.2 requires comparing and ordering decimal fractions to the thousandths with <, >, =, establishing decimal place-value magnitude and relative-position judgment; B5.1.4.1.3 requires rounding decimals to the nearest tenth and hundredth, which operationally depends on judging which benchmark value a decimal is nearer to. Proficiency in comparing/ordering decimals therefore supports success in rounding decimals, a substantive same-rank developmental direction rather than mere code adjacency or page proximity. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (rank 2, same grade coordinate) under Content Standard B6.4.1.1 'Create, label, and interpret line graphs to draw conclusions', so the same-rank direction rests on statement content, not code order. B6.4.1.1.1 establishes the constructive skill: determine a line graph's common attributes (title, axes, intervals) and draw the graph from a given table of values. B6.4.1.1.3 explicitly 'Apply[s] understanding of how to create a line graph' from a given table of values and then extends to answering questions to interpret and draw conclusions. The shared Learning Component 'Draw a line graph for a given table of values' is claimed by both, while the second adds the distinct interpretive component 'Answer questions based on a line graph to interpret it and draw conclusions'. Proficiency in constructing the graph therefore supports success in the applied interpretation indicator; direction first_to_second. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same coordinate rank 0) in Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations, so the grain and domain match. First (B4.2.2.1.1) requires writing a given problem as an equation in which a symbol represents an unknown number; second (B4.2.2.2.4) requires solving a given one-step equation by 'guess and check' under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 'Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number'. Beyond shared wording, there is substantive same-rank developmental evidence: fluency in representing an unknown by a symbol within an equation is the formulation skill on which the solving indicator operates, since guess-and-check requires interpreting the symbol as an unknown value to be found. This supports likelihood of success rather than strict prerequisite ordering, hence buildsTowards from the representation indicator to the solving indicator. Judgment is bounded by truncated source evidence (24 omitted items per endpoint) and upstream audit/merge context on both endpoints and their ancestors.

B5.1.3.1.6 asks learners to use models to explain multiplying a fraction by a whole number, while B5.1.3.1.3 asks learners to apply equivalent fractions to obtain a common denominator for adding and subtracting like fractions (LCs: addition/subtraction with equivalent fractions vs. modelling fraction-by-whole-number multiplication). judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit under the same BASIC 5 Content Standard B5.3.1.1 (identify and sort quadrilaterals by attributes) in Sub-Strand 'Lines and Shapes'. B5.3.1.1.1 (second) establishes understanding of specific shape properties — sides, angles and diagonals of squares and rectangles — as shown by its LCs on squares and rectangles. B5.3.1.1.3 (first) generalises that attribute work into a justification task: proving any polygon is regular by measuring its sides and angles or by folding/superimposing, with LCs covering both the measuring and folding methods. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Content Standards (same grain, identical rank 2, gap 0) under Strand 1: Number but in different Sub-Strands: B6.1.2.2 'Demonstrate understanding of multiplication of a 2 or 3-digit number by a 2 or 3-digit number' (Number Operations) and B6.1.4.2 'Understand the concept of proportion and its relationship to ratios and rates... use proportional reasoning and rates to solve real-world and mathematical problems' (Ratios and Proportion). There is genuine multiplicative-reasoning coherence: multi-digit multiplication fluency is the computational partner of scaling, rates and proportion problem solving, so the two reinforce each other meaningfully. However, at equal grade rank the supplied text offers no substantive evidence that one is developmentally dependent on the other (the proportion standard is conceptual and does not reference multi-digit multiplication procedures, and no Learning Components were supplied for either endpoint), so symmetric relatesTo rather than a directional buildsTowards is warranted. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same rank 0) in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis), so direction rests on statement substance rather than rank. The second (B4.4.1.1.3, under Content Standard B4.4.1.1 'Demonstrate an understanding of many-to-one correspondence in displaying, and reading or interpreting, graphs') has learners compare graphs displaying the same data and explain how they are the same and different — analytic attention to graph features. The first (B4.4.1.2.1, under Content Standard B4.4.1.2 'Construct and interpret pictographs and bar graphs involving many-to-one correspondence') explicitly requires identifying common features of many-to-one graphs and then using that understanding to construct bar graphs or pictographs with title, labelled axes and key/legend for up to 4 categories. Proficiency in comparing/explaining graph similarities and differences plausibly supports success in the construction task, which names feature identification as its entry point; the shift from interpreting existing displays to producing conventioned displays is a substantive extension, not mere repetition. Shared LC tokens ('data', 'graphs') and the weak code-prefix/rank-proximity signals were treated as nomination reasons only. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the full exemplar text was not available.

The first models number quantities up to 1,000,000 with graph sheets and multi-base blocks (LC tags: model, multi-base, place value); the second compares and orders whole numbers up to 100,000 and records comparisons with >, <, = (LCs: compare whole numbers, order whole numbers, represent the comparison symbolically; tag: place value). These are complementary place-value treatments of whole-number magnitude — concrete representation alongside relational comparison and symbolic recording — giving substantive, instructionally useful coherence beyond shared wording. However, no pair-specific evidence establishes a developmental dependency or direction: the two are same-rank siblings, the only ordering signal is the source code sequence (not admissible as developmental evidence), and the comparison indicator's range (100,000) is narrower than the modelling indicator's (1,000,000), so no substantive increase in demand is demonstrated. Canonical symmetric relatesTo with null direction is therefore the correct complete judgment. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and endpoints/ancestors carry upstream audit/merge/code context, so this rests on the bounded statement text, Learning Components, and hierarchy shown.

judgment.rationale: Both Indicators sit under the same BASIC 4 Content Standard B4.2.2.2 ("Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number") in Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations, and both are at coordinate rank 0 (BASIC 4), so direction rests on statement content rather than grade. B4.2.2.2.2 asks learners to describe orally the meaning of a given one-step equation with one unknown (LC tags: meaning, one-step equation, oral description, unknown), i.e. interpreting what the equation asserts about the unknown. B4.2.2.2.4 asks learners to solve a given one-step equation using "guess and check" (LC tags: equations, guess and check, one-step), which requires substituting trial values and judging whether the equation is satisfied — an operation that depends on understanding the equation's meaning. Proficiency in interpreting the equation therefore supports success in the trial-and-verify solution strategy, supporting second_to_first; the reverse (solving procedurally supporting oral interpretation) is less directly supported by the texts. Shared wording alone ("given", "one-step", "equation") was not treated as sufficient; the judgment rests on the interpret-then-solve content distinction. Both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each), so bounded exemplar detail may qualify this reading.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 Indicators (same coordinate rank 1) under Strand 4: Data, Sub-Strand 1 'Data Collection, Organisation, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis', but sit under different Content Standards: B5.4.1.1 (differentiate first-hand vs second-hand data) and B5.4.1.2 (construct and interpret double bar graphs). The first indicator has learners locate examples of second-hand data in print/electronic media (LC tags: data collection, media, second-hand data); the second has learners draw and use double bar graphs with title, labelled axes and legend for up to 3 paired categories (LC tags: data representation, double bar graph, solve problems). They are complementary stages of the same data-handling cycle — sourcing/recognising data and representing/interpreting it — giving substantive conceptual coherence, but the bounded evidence shows no statement-level dependency: graphing double bar graphs is not stated to require identifying second-hand media sources, and the two are same-rank peers, so no developmental direction is substantiated. Textual/LC overlap is limited to the generic token 'data' (Jaccard ~0.05–0.08), and code-prefix/page proximity are weak signals only, so relatesTo rather than buildsTowards.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Content Standards in Strand 2: Algebra (same grain, same resolved rank 0), but sit in different sub-strands: B4.2.1.1 (Patterns and Relationships) asks learners to identify and describe patterns in tables and charts including a multiplication chart, while B4.2.2.2 (Unknowns, Expressions and Equations) asks learners to solve one-step equations using a symbol for an unknown. These are complementary strands of early algebraic reasoning — recognising regularity in tabular/multiplication structure supports meaning-making about number relationships used when solving for an unknown — but the bounded evidence (no Learning Components supplied, truncated source evidence, distinct sub-strand parents, identical grade rank) does not substantiate that proficiency in one is developmentally required or reliably supportive for the other in a specific direction. Shared Strand/Grade ancestry, weak code-prefix overlap (b4, 2) and token overlap limited to stopwords ('a','an','to') carry no directional weight, so the symmetric coherence judgment is the supported one.

judgment.rationale: Both are Indicators under the same Content Standard B4.2.2.2 ('Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number'), Sub-Strand 'Unknowns, Expressions and Equations', Strand Algebra, at the same BASIC 4 coordinate (rank 0), so same-grain comparison applies and direction rests on statement substance, not rank. B4.2.2.2.4 requires solving a given one-step equation with a 'guess and check' strategy — operating on an equation whose unknown must be found. B4.2.2.2.7 requires creating a problem for a given equation with one unknown, i.e. interpreting the equation's structure and translating it into a contextual problem, a substantively more demanding reverse-translation task that presumes the learner can already work with and satisfy a one-step equation containing an unknown (LC tags: 'equations/one-step/guess and check' vs 'equation/problem/unknown/word problem'). Proficiency in solving such equations therefore supports likely success in posing problems for them; the shared parent, code prefix, page proximity and token overlap are treated only as nomination signals. Evidence limitation: source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so the full exemplars behind each indicator were not available, which moderates confidence.

Shared 'referents' wording plus the sub-strand/measurement context, not code prefixes alone, supports this. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (same grade rank 2) in Strand 1: Number, Sub-Strand 4: Ratios and Proportion, so the statement-type grain matches. The first (B6.1.4.1.1) establishes the ratio concept itself via concrete models and pictorial representations, plus symbolic writing and simplest form (LCs: 'use concrete models... to explain a ratio', 'write a ratio symbolically', 'write a ratio in its simplest form'). The second (B6.1.4.2.1) uses models to explain proportion 'as a comparison between quantities with equal ratios', i.e., it explicitly presupposes and extends the ratio concept into equality of ratios, mirrored by its parent Content Standard B6.1.4.2 ('concept of proportion and its relationship to ratios and rates'). Despite equal grade rank, the substantive evidence is directional: proficiency in representing and simplifying ratios supports success in reasoning about proportion as equal ratios, so first_to_second is justified rather than symmetric relatesTo. Shared modeling language and code prefix alone were not treated as sufficient.

judgment.rationale: Both are Indicator-grain statements at the same BASIC 6 coordinate (rank 2) under Content Standard B6.4.1.1 'Create, label, and interpret line graphs to draw conclusions' (Strand 4: Data). The second SFI (B6.4.1.1.1, LCs 'determine the common attributes (title, axes and intervals) of a line graph' and 'draw a line graph for a given table of values') establishes the constructive skill of building a line graph from tabulated values. The first SFI (B6.4.1.1.2, LCs 'determine whether a given set of data can be represented by a line graph (continuous data) or a series of points (discrete data)' and 'explain why') is a substantively more demanding judgement/justification task about representational appropriateness, which presupposes knowing how line graphs are structured and plotted. Since ranks are equal, direction rests on this pair-specific content escalation from construction to evaluative reasoning about continuous vs discrete data, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first. Evidence limitation: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (24 omitted items each) and shared ancestry/code prefix alone was not treated as supporting evidence.

judgment.rationale: B4.4.1.2 (Strand 4 Data, Sub-strand 1) asks learners to construct and interpret pictographs and bar graphs involving many-to-one correspondence, while B4.1.2.4 (Strand 1 Number, Sub-strand 2 Number Operations) asks for recall of basic division facts up to 100. Interpreting a many-to-one scale (e.g. one symbol represents several items) is inherently multiplicative/divisive reasoning, so the two statements share substantive skill coherence and mutually reinforce multiplicative fact fluency applied in a data-representation context. Both sit at the same resolved coordinate BASIC 4 (rank 0) in different strands, and the bounded evidence (nomination is mostly grade co-location, weak code-prefix 'b4', and trivial token/trigram overlap such as 'to') gives no substantive basis to assert that proficiency in one is developmentally required for the other, so a symmetric relatesTo rather than a same-rank buildsTowards is warranted. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (26 and 24 omitted items), which limits deeper confirmation; the merge note on c286f653 records only that the Basic 4 code is distinct from an identically worded Basic 5 item.

The first SFI (B5.3.2.2.3) applies and extends that skill to a comparative/constructive task: generating multiple differently shaped boxes that hold the same volume, which presupposes being able to determine a box's volume in unit cubes and hold that quantity invariant across different dimensions (the source context for the first cites an exemplar 'Given 12 centimetre...' cubes). These are complementary skills for the same pattern-rule goal: one supplies a visual representation used to check predicted continuations, the other evaluates and justifies a specific candidate continuation. Neither subsumes or escalates the other, and the bounded evidence gives no pair-specific indication that proficiency in the visual-representation indicator increases likelihood of success in the explain-why indicator (or vice versa) beyond a generic cognitive argument; the direction is genuinely symmetric, so same-rank buildsTowards is not justified. B6.1.1.1.3 concerns locating numbers in positions around a given number on a number chart (number-sequence and relative-position sense); B6.1.1.1.5 concerns rounding whole numbers up to 100,000 to nearest ten thousands/thousands/hundreds/tens, whose LCs tag place value and round off/up/down. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same grain, same rank 0) under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 'Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number' in Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations. The second SFI (B4.2.2.2.2) asks learners to describe orally the meaning of a given one-step equation with one unknown — interpreting what the equation and its unknown represent; the first (B4.2.2.2.3) asks learners to solve a given equation when the unknown sits on the left or right side. Being able to articulate the meaning of an equation and locate/interpret the unknown substantively supports the more demanding procedural task of solving such equations regardless of the unknown's position, so the same-rank developmental direction runs from the interpretive indicator to the solving indicator (LC tags confirm: 'meaning, one-step equation, oral description, unknown' vs 'equation, one-step, solve, unknown'). Shared parentage, code prefix, and page proximity alone were not treated as sufficient; the statement texts carry the judgment. Source evidence for both endpoints is truncated (24 omitted items each), so exemplar detail is unavailable.

judgment.rationale: Both endpoints are BASIC 4 Indicators (rank 0, same grade coordinate) in Strand 1 NUMBER, Sub-strand 3: Fractions, so any developmental direction would need substantive same-rank evidence. B4.1.3.2.1 concerns comparing and ordering like-denominator fractions via pictorial representations and equivalent fractions with the LCD (LCs: compare/order fractions, LCD, pictorial), while B4.1.3.1.4 concerns recognising, drawing and labelling improper fractions (LCs: recognise/draw/label improper fractions). These are complementary Basic 4 fraction-representation skills that reinforce one another (pictorial modelling and symbolic labelling of fractions), but neither statement's proficiency is shown by the bounded evidence to be a substantive enabler of the other: improper-fraction recognition is not required to compare like-denominator fractions, and comparing/ordering does not extend into improper-fraction notation. Source code prefix, page proximity and the single shared token 'fractions' are weak nomination signals only, and the parent Content Standards carry a known Basic 4 Fractions editorial code anomaly (B4.1.3.1/B4.1.3.2 merge context), which further weakens any code-order-based directional inference. Symmetric conceptual coherence is supported; dependency is not.
